runs.text: The cherry on top, and the finishing touches

slides.notes: The last day of the program. Students have written their introductions, theses, body paragraphs and conclusions; all that’s left is the title. The title is the cherry on top of the ice cream sundae that is a great essay. We’ve all seen "English Essay" and "My Paper." Our students have invested real time in something original, so they deserve a title that is too.

slides.notes: The one question students still get wrong: some cling to "a good conclusion restates the thesis." Here’s the structure again for anyone still finishing. The Tutor shows this structure in its box too.
Now the title. A lot of people dread it, but with the colon-title model it becomes pretty easy and quick.

runs.text: Don’t ever, ever, EVER title your essay “Essay” or “English Paper.” Let it indicate your topic in a thoughtful way. Try the colon title:
Beyond the Boys’ Club: How Female Heroes Define the Avengers Legacy
Bored in the USA: How Lack of Creativity in Schools Hurts Students and Teachers
Unlocked and Loaded: How Easy Gun Access Puts Children at Risk

slides.notes: Read the three aloud. With each one we know exactly what the essay is about, and it makes us want to read it. The second is the sample essay’s.

runs.text: How Female Heroes Define the Avengers Legacy
Left of the colon · creative, fun:
Right of the colon · clear, direct:
How Female Heroes Define the Avengers Legacy

slides.notes: Each title has two parts. The left side is a creative or "fun" element; the right side delivers a clear, direct description of the topic. Alone, each would be ordinary at best and confusing at worst: "Beyond the Boys’ Club" could be about single-sex schools, fraternities, men in politics… The right side gives it context; the left side gives the right side flavor. The right side doesn’t have to start with "How" (all three just happen to). The Tutor knows the colon title too and can help students draft and revise theirs.

runs.text: : your title is about the same thing
say clearly what your essay is about
something creative, like a phrase, a pun or an image
for feedback, then try a second version

slides.notes: Give them about five minutes. On the Title Your Essay! step the Tutor walks them through the colon title and gives feedback on drafts. Have a few students read theirs aloud; vote on favorites if the room is into it. A title without a colon is fine too, as long as it is informative, smart and memorable.
The last stretch: clean up the document, put the title on it, format it simply, and submit.

slides.notes: Brian: "Be normal with your formatting. This is not the place to be creative." Some students like to center everything or pick fancy fonts; don’t. If you have your own formatting standard, use it. Then celebrate: ask students for a reflection on the process, or have them highlight their favorite part of their essay and add a comment saying why. Share the work: within the class, with other teachers or administrators. (The YAWP! program can also publish a class’s essays as a printed book.)
